summary: Describes the problem statement for Configuration and Provisioning for Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP), the need to configure and manage many wireless access points centrally.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes difficulties that arise when an enterprise manages many wireless access points. It identifies reasons to consider an interoperable interface between access points and central controllers.

questions: why is managing many wifi boxes hard
why is managing many wireless access points hard
subtitle: Problems that arise when managing and provisioning large wireless LANs.

tldr.problem: Large wireless LAN deployments make access-point management, consistent configuration, radio coordination and physical security difficult.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes a need for an interoperable interface between wireless access points and centralized controllers.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is a problem statement that identifies issues and security requirements; it does not specify a CAPWAP protocol.

today: RFC 3990 is Informational and describes problems in wireless access-point configuration and provisioning. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Growth of Large Wireless LANs
sections.content:
The RFC traces enterprise wireless LAN deployments to the IEEE approval of 802.11 in 1997 and amendments 802.11a and 802.11b in 1999. It says larger deployments, including some with several thousand access points, created management problems.

Each access point is an IP-addressable device. Large deployments can increase the number of infrastructure devices to manage, and nearly identical configurations can still lead to misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: Large wireless networks may contain many access points, each requiring management. Similar settings across devices can still be applied inconsistently.

sections.title: Problems in Large Deployments
sections.content:
The memo identifies four problems. Administrators must manage and monitor each access point; distributing a consistent configuration takes time; the shared wireless medium requires coordinated monitoring and adjustment; and securing access points is difficult when they are installed outside locked rooms.

The RFC notes that theft of an access point containing embedded secrets can expose resources protected by those secrets. It also describes the burden of manually monitoring wireless conditions and determining new settings for many access points.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrators must keep access points configured consistently and coordinate their use of shared radio space. Devices in exposed locations also create physical security concerns.

sections.title: Need for an Interoperable Interface
sections.content:
The RFC says multiple vendors had begun offering proprietary solutions combining network switching, centralized control and distributed wireless access. Those solutions were not interoperable because vendors made different architectural choices.

The memo describes a system with one or more access points and one or more central control devices, also called access controllers. It says a standardized, interoperable interface could let network designers choose access points and controllers from different vendors.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo calls for an interface that works across access points and central controllers. It describes this need without defining the interface protocol.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
Because wireless access points control network access and deliver packets, the RFC says their control and provisioning functions need protection. Requirements should address confidentiality, integrity and authenticity for central management, monitoring and control.

The memo raises questions about whether one level of authorization is enough after an access point and controller authenticate each other. It notes that storing high-value secrets in a controller may reduce the consequences of a stolen access point, while concentrating those secrets makes the controller an attractive target that needs strong controls.
sections.plainLanguage: Management of access points needs protections for confidentiality, integrity and authenticity. The RFC notes that storing secrets centrally can protect them from a stolen access point but increases the value of the controller to an attacker.
